newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech leaders turn up heat on cabinet talks.
newsitem.headline: Czech leaders turn up heat on cabinet talks.

text.p: Czech political leaders turned up the heat in talks on reconstructing their beleaguered cabinet on Wednesday, with currency markets awaiting the outcome and its impact on the weakened crown.
Czech Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus cancelled a day trip to the Netherlands to continue talks with his partners in the centre-right ruling coalition, Klaus's office said.

The leaders of the three coalition parties ended a morning meeting and were to report to their individual party leaderships about the state of the coalition talks, government spokesman Ivo Strejcek told journalists.
Klaus was scheduled to attend a ceremony marking the 50th anniversary of the Marshall Plan in the Hague.
The government has also cancelled its regular Wednesday meeting, Strejcek said.

The coalition leaders agreed last week to make changes in the cabinet after a sharp drop in the government's approval rating spurred by an economic downturn, and numerous reports of financial crimes and banking failures.
The crown lost about eight percent of its value on Tuesday after speculators' attacks forced the central bank on Monday to allow it to float.
Currency traders said they were anxiously following the coalition talks to give support to the crown or allow it to fall further.

"The Czech crown is waiting for what will happen on the political side of things," said trader Milan Vavra of Komercni Banka. "Political destabilisation is the most important thing for foreign investors so nobody is doing a lot of business in foreign exchange," he said.
On Tuesday evening the leaders began discussing a declaration on the government programme which would accompany the changes.
The Czech news agency CTK reported on Wednesday that overnight meetings of the junior parties in the coalition revealed a major split in opinions on the declaration.

It quoted Civic Democratic Alliance (ODA) chairman Michael Zantovsky as flatly rejecting a proposal by Christian Democrat (KDU-CSL) leader Josef Lux to introduce import surcharges to relieve a massive trade deficit which has put pressure on the crown.

"If the decision by the central bank was moving toward a fixed exchange rate, then an import surcharge would have some sense," Zantovsky said. "Of course since the crown rate is floating then it makes no economic sense."
Klaus on Tuesday said he would push for a rapid reconstruction of the cabinet to try to end the political uncertainty.
